title: Fiat-Shamir Attacks Are Not Misuse, the Protocol Itself Is Unsound
dek: Protocols actually deployed, like GKR, can be proven to accept false statements under standard Fiat-Shamir; this is not an implementation oversight, it is a problem with the transform itself.
why: The first half's theory review is slow, but the construction of the Fiat-Shamir attack and the measured numbers from Flock and snark.fast are worth hearing.
who: Engineers building ZK proof systems, SNARKs or ZKVMs, and researchers concerned with Fiat-Shamir security and AI-assisted engineering optimization.
skip: The opening chat about the difference between theorists and practitioners (around 3:00-6:00) can be skipped.

points.body: Before Ron's work with Lev and Dmitry, the community already knew there existed examples of ‘secure interactive protocol + Fiat-Shamir = total collapse’, but those protocols were deliberately constructed by theorists to prove Fiat-Shamir doesn't always hold, and looked extremely unnatural. The typical industry reaction was ‘our real protocols wouldn't do something that stupid’. Ron himself had made a semi-artificial example a few years earlier, one component of which was fictional, which kept him doubtful about security. The turning point was the bug bounty the Ethereum Foundation set up while researching Poseidon's security, whose final tier was ‘launch a Fiat-Shamir attack on any protocol of your choice using Poseidon’. Ron didn't go for the prize; instead he suggested changing the terms to ‘non-fictional protocols’, which directly led to the investigation of real deployed protocols.

points.h: GKR's data-saving feature became the attack surface
points.body: What was actually broken was the GKR protocol, widely used in practice; Polyhedra's Expander system uses it. The attack exploits a real feature of GKR: it allows ‘recording less data’, seemingly recording less, but implicitly confirming that data—this is exactly why people want to use GKR, and exactly this feature makes the attack possible. The key condition for the attack to work is: the depth of the circuit being proven (the scheme) must be at least as deep as the depth of the hash function used in Fiat-Shamir, and implementations at the time had no restriction on this. Polyhedra made changes and paid the bounty.

points.h: The mitigation is just making the hash chain deeper
points.body: The mitigation is plain: make the hash function slightly deeper than the circuit being proven. Concretely, chain multiple Poseidons together, do 10 Poseidons, and the circuit naturally becomes 10 times deeper, with no expected trick to bypass it. That's how Polyhedra changed it. But Ron explicitly stresses this is only a mitigation—we can't demonstrate an attack, but we also don't know whether an attack truly doesn't exist. This differs from common Fiat-Shamir vulnerabilities: those are usually misuse in practice, like forgetting to include some prover-sent messages in the hash; this time it's still insecure even when Fiat-Shamir is used correctly per spec.

points.h: Diagonalization: making a program take itself as input
points.body: Ron gives an extremely artificial protocol to illustrate the attack principle: the prover sends a message M, the verifier runs M as program code with input also M, waits for it to output a 100-bit string, then compares with 100 random bits, accepting only if they match. Interactively this protocol is almost impossible to accept, because once M is sent, M(M) is fully determined, and the probability of hitting 100 random bits is 2 to the negative 100. But with Fiat-Shamir, the random bits become H(M), and the prover only needs to find M satisfying M(M) = H(M)—take M to be the hash function H itself, since M(M) = H(H) = H(M). This kind of trick is called diagonalization, essentially forcing a program to nest itself.

Blaze, Tensor Switch, and Bolt are all hash-based polynomial commitment schemes, sharing a reliance on error-correcting codes. FRI, STIR, WHIR are all built on Reed-Solomon codes, while these three projects try to trade better error-correcting codes for better PCS. Bolt uses a code called sketched code: first take a non-cryptographic ‘digest’ of the message, apply Reed-Solomon encoding only to the digest, and the overall codeword = encoding of the digest + original message. The benefit is that Reed-Solomon acts only on data about one-tenth the size, cutting encoding cost by an order of magnitude. The cost may be larger proof size, but in scenarios where not everyone needs to read the proof, proving time matters more. Ron points out this line focuses on proving efficiency, while the WHIR line focuses on verification and proof size, and the two can coexist via proof composition: use Bolt to get extremely fast proving, then recursively prove its verifier with WHIR, inheriting high-quality verification.

points.h: Veil gives hash-based proofs native zero-knowledge
points.body: Veil is a method to make a certain class of hash-based proof systems zero-knowledge (Ron dislikes the term ZK ZK). Traditionally, implementing zero-knowledge in SP1 means recursively composing a succinct proof with Groth16, but Groth16 is not post-quantum secure. Veil wants a native, hash-based zero-knowledge scheme. Existing proofs of concept show that both proving time and proof size overhead are quite small, and the plan is to implement it directly in SP1.

points.h: Flock lets Ethereum dare to abandon Poseidon
points.body: Flock is a proof system for batch verification of Boolean circuits, developed by Ron with Benedict and their student William Lang, pushing theory toward practicality. Ron believes it brought a ‘second spring’ to the industry, and more importantly spawned a large number of new ideas and follow-up research. One direct consequence is the Ethereum Foundation's decision to move from Poseidon to some kind of Boolean hash. Before Flock, it wasn't clear this could be done efficiently; Flock plus Binius's important early influence proved it feasible. Ron attributes this shift to two things happening at once: first, the new attack shook people's confidence in Poseidon, and second, something that seemed surprising a year earlier—traditional hash functions are actually quite efficient to use in proofs.

points.h: Swapping the prover doesn't break soundness, only threatens completeness
points.body: snark.fast is a collaboration between Zcash, Igalia Labs (leading), the Ethereum Foundation, and Espresso, with the idea of keeping the Plonk verifier unchanged and only replacing the prover, to see how much faster it can get. Ron distinguishes two properties: soundness means no one can convince you to accept a false statement, so no matter how fast a prover you make, false statements can't be proven, and in that sense there's no security problem; completeness means true statements must be provable, which is harder to guarantee, and snark.fast only guarantees that proofs are still accepted on random inputs. A more ambitious approach is to prove that the changes don't alter the prover's input-output behavior, which is exactly the goal pursued by ZK-Golf and Kobe et al., with stronger completeness guarantees. Ron also worries that these fully AI-driven projects, lacking oversight, could have AI slip malicious code into the prover.

points.h: AI found an unused GPU on the Mac
points.body: Ron originally expected this kind of large-scale crowdsourced AI to bring 10-20% engineering improvement; the actual result was 2.5 to 3 times, and purely engineering optimization, with no protocol changes. One interesting episode is that AI noticed early on that tests were running on a Mac, and the Mac had an unused GPU—not that it didn't know it existed, but that previous attempts to use it hadn't worked well; AI was clearly better at using it, contributing significantly to success. Another surprise was the later x86 version, e.g., executing SNARKs on Intel servers without a GPU, more than 3 times faster than their Falcon implementation. One specific optimization technique is memory scanning: if an algorithm needs to scan memory twice to do two things, changing it to do both in one pass saves a lot of work; they knew to do this, but AI did it better.

points.h: An AI built a processor simulator to compete
points.body: snark.fast targets specific hardware (roughly the M3 processor), and people without that processor couldn't participate. So an AI built a simulator for that processor to get its work accepted. Ron even worried at one point that some AI had hacked the snark.fast website to fake data, because that's exactly what it was programmed to do. The evaluation mechanism itself is key to making this approach work: someone submits a faster prover, it's run on a large number of random inputs to see if it can make the original June Flock verifier accept, and if it does, it counts as valid, then timing over many experiments is measured, and faster means new leader. This part is managed by Igalia Labs on the Yukon platform. ZK-Golf takes another path: instead of changing prover engineering, it changes the scheme itself, expressing schemes in a Lean-based DSL (Clean) and verifying their soundness and completeness; people have already added binary field and Flock-style schemes, with large percentage improvements over the scheme in the original Flock paper.

points.h: Proving a hash is only 200 times slower than computing one
points.body: Ron's long-term goal is ‘proving as fast as computation’, and he wrote an article in 2020 called Proving as Fast as Computation. Measured with Flock, proving a bunch of hashes is only about 200 times slower than directly computing hashes—sounds like a lot, but far faster than previously thought. He cautions that the meaning of this number needs careful interpretation. The next step is to use new ideas from snark.fast, ZK-Golf, and Flock V2 to keep pushing this multiple down, aiming for 1x. If that can really be achieved, it means all computation in the world becomes verifiable: your agent, someone else's agent, any operation by anyone, can be verified against a baseline at extremely low cost to confirm it was done correctly, including machine learning training and inference. Ron also mentions that perhaps the universe has some inherent limit preventing proving from being as fast as computation, and proving that would be equally cool.

terms.def: A transform that turns an interactive protocol into a non-interactive one, replacing the verifier's random coin flips with a hash function.
An interactive protocol for proving circuit correctness, widely used because it allows recording less data.
A trick that makes a program nest itself as input, thereby constructing an input satisfying a specific equation.
Captures a large polynomial with a tiny commitment, later allowing proofs about computations on that polynomial; a core component of SNARKs.
An error-correcting code that first takes a short digest of the message and applies Reed-Solomon encoding only to the digest, making encoding faster.
Finite fields with elements 0/1, promoted by Binius for use in proof systems, with Nvidia GPUs now adding support.

Mhm. And it was this feature that made it possible to carry out our attack.

So, Plonk correctness generally means that if you have a false statement, no one should be able to convince you to accept it. Good. Yes? In particular, neither Snark.fast nor Snark.faster nor Snark.fastest—no one should be able to convince you of something that is false.

I thought it was pretty obvious that using such massive crowdsourcing AI would yield better engineering than what we had with our agent and a small number of tokens. And I was expecting, you know, 10-20% or something like that. They actually achieved two and a half or three times better results.

What it means is that all computations in the world become verifiable. Anything that anybody, your agent, anybody else's agent, anything that anybody does -- yeah, that you can compare to a baseline to very cheaply verify that it was done correctly.
